intro.heading: The policy is right now. Is the practice?
intro.sub: A scenario we see in many care settings.
intro.paragraph: A resident fell in the lounge late one evening and was found by a carer on a routine round. She was not badly hurt, but the manager looked hard at what happened and decided the falls prevention policy needed a clearer first step after a fall. She drafted the change, a second pair of eyes read it, and it went through the approval your service has set up. The new version is live. It is a good result, and it is not the end. A policy only protects people when the team who use it know what changed, and at the moment nobody can say whether they do.

trail.text: A resident falls in the lounge and is found on a routine round.
The manager reviews what happened and decides the policy needs a clearer first step.
The change is approved and the new version goes live.
The new version is on the system. Nobody has checked who has read it.
Two night carers and a bank carer who have not been on shift since the change.
A newer carer who reads the policy once and mixes up the old step with the new one.
An approved version and a date. Nothing that shows the team understood it.
“What do you do first?” The answer is the old one.

trail_close: The approval was never the problem. The gap sits between a signed off policy and what staff do on shift. Here is how CareStream handles the route from incident to understanding, without pretending the system does your thinking for you.

why.heading: A new version is a document. Understanding is the outcome.
why.sub: After an incident, the question that matters is whether practice changed.

cards.title: A version number tells nobody what changed
cards.body: Staff who open the new policy may not spot the one step that moved. The change that came from a real incident is easy to read past.

cards.title: Approval proves the paperwork, not the team
cards.body: Sign off shows the right people reviewed the text. It cannot show that the night team, or a carer on their second week, understood it.

cards.title: Briefing by hand is patchy
cards.body: A talk at handover reaches whoever is in the room. People on other shifts miss it, and nobody records what anyone took away.

talk.heading: The questions managers ask, and how CareStream answers them
talk.sub: Read this as a conversation. The questions are the ones we hear most.

items.q: Our policy changed after an incident. What does CareStream do with the change?
items.a: You adopt the change as a tracked edit on a draft, and it goes through your approval chain before it is published. Once it is live, staff reading and the staff assistant use the new text. Approval and sign off are on Professional and above.

items.q: Who has to approve a policy change?
items.a: It depends on how you set it up. An admin approves first, then the care manager step is on by default, and an external reviewer by one off link is an option you can switch on. If nothing else is switched on, it publishes straight away after the admin.

items.q: What if I only fix a typo?
items.a: A typo or proofreading fix can be made as a minor edit. It skips the approval chain, is recorded as a tracked change and does not reset anything. A real change to what staff do goes through approval.

items.q: Does CareStream tell staff when a policy changes?
items.a: Not automatically. A new version going live does not send staff a message. To brief your team you allocate short training on the topic, which is the step that makes sure people have seen and understood the change.

items.q: How do I check people understood the change?
items.a: You allocate a topic module, such as Falls Prevention, built from your own policies. Each carer completes it in the Staff Hub, and a wrong answer goes to their Follow-up tab. They open a short lesson with Learn & retry, then answer a fresh question. They can retry as often as they like.

items.q: Can I choose the exact policy that changed?
items.a: No. You choose a topic module and CareStream draws on your policies for that topic. Because the new version is the live one, the training reflects the changed wording. You can edit and preview the module before staff see it.

items.q: What do I see across the team?
items.a: The Knowledge gaps view shows the questions most often missed, the weakest topics and how gaps are being closed, and a digest arrives on Monday. That tells you whether one person needs a conversation or the policy wording needs another look.

limits.heading: Support for good policy governance, not a substitute for it

cards.title: It does not decide what the change should be
cards.body: Suggested wording is a starting point your admin adopts, edits and sends through approval. Nothing is changed automatically, and it is not legal advice.

cards.title: It does not message staff when a version goes live
cards.body: A new version does not alert your team by itself. CareStream records reading sessions, not signatures, so you brief people through allocated training.

cards.title: The approval chain and gap fixes need Professional
cards.body: Adopting changes and the approval trail are on Professional and above. Allocating adhoc training is on the paid plans, and the free plan does not include it.

items.q: What is policy change management in a care service?
items.a: It is the route a policy takes from a reason to change, such as an incident, through drafting, review, approval and publishing, to staff understanding the change. The last step is the one most services skip.

items.q: How does policy approval work in CareStream?
items.a: A change is adopted onto a draft, an admin approves it, then the care manager step applies unless you switch it off, and an external reviewer can be added by one off link. Rejected changes go back to draft with a note. This is on Professional and above.

items.q: What does policy sign off involve?
items.a: Your own approval chain is the sign off, and the trail is kept. You can also print a policy on your letterhead with a sign off block for registered manager, approved by, date approved and next review.

items.q: How does policy version control work?
items.a: Real changes create a new major version with a read only snapshot, and the History tab lists earlier versions. Document version history is on every plan. A minor edit, such as a typo, does not start a new approval.

items.q: Who is responsible for policy governance?
items.a: The provider is. The law asks registered providers to operate systems to assess, monitor and improve quality and safety, and to keep the records needed. See Regulation 17 on good governance. CareStream gives you a place to run that process, not the duty itself.

items.q: What is policy training, and does CareStream do it?
items.a: Policy training means making sure staff know and can apply the policy. CareStream builds short training from your own policies, checks it with questions and turns wrong answers into short lessons. A competent person still shows practical skills.

items.q: Does an incident mean staff need retraining?
items.a: Not always. If the change affects what people do, a short check is sensible. Our guide on who needs retraining gives four questions to decide.

items.q: What does the law say about training and risk?
items.a: Providers must assess risks and do all that is reasonably practicable to mitigate them, and make sure staff have the competence and skills to provide care safely. See Regulation 12 on safe care and treatment. Staff must also receive the support and training they need, in Regulation 18.

items.q: Can I use this for a falls prevention policy change?
items.a: Yes, it is a good fit. The Falls Prevention topic module is built from your policies once the new version is live. Pair it with the moving and handling course for the hands on side.

guide.heading: A practical route from incident to understanding
guide.lede: Whatever tools you use, these steps keep policy change management clear and calm after something goes wrong.

sections.h3: Decide what the incident really changes
paragraphs: Start with the fact, not the fix. Write one plain sentence on what happened and one on what staff should now do differently. If you cannot write the second sentence, the policy may not need to change yet.
Keep the change small and specific. A policy that moves one step is easier to brief and easier to check than one that was rewritten end to end.

sections.h3: Run the change through the right approval
paragraphs: Match the level of approval to the size of the change. A typo is a minor edit. A change to what carers do deserves a second reader, and your care manager or an outside reviewer where you use one. Keep the reason for the change on the record. See policy version control for the habits that stop old versions circulating.
checklist: Name the incident and the date in the change note
Have the change read by someone who did not write it
Approve it through the chain your service has set up
Publish it and confirm staff can see the new version

sections.h3: Brief people and check it landed
paragraphs: Publishing is not briefing. Within a few days, give every affected carer, including nights and part time staff, a short check on the change. Look at the most missed questions, and go back to the policy wording if the same point trips several people. For more, see our guide to incident led training and updating policies after big changes.

guide.note: This guide is general good practice, not legal advice. Check your own duties and your regulator's guidance for your service.
